title: How the Car Changed Everyday Life
summary: A hundred years ago, city streets were full of horses and very smelly. Cars cleaned up the streets, let families live in new suburbs, and invented whole new places like motels, drive-in movies and shopping malls. Cars gave many people freedom, but highways also cut through neighbourhoods, and not everyone could travel safely.

sections.heading: When Cities Ran on Horses
paragraphs: Close your eyes and imagine walking down a busy street in New York, London or Chicago in about 1890. You hear the clatter of iron horseshoes and wooden wheels on stone. Horse-drawn buses, delivery wagons, cabs, brewers' carts and fire engines crowd the road. And you smell it before you see it: horses, everywhere, and everything horses leave behind.

Big cities around 1900 were home to tens of thousands of working horses, and the largest had many more. They pulled almost everything. They also produced an astonishing amount of waste. A working horse makes roughly 7 to 15 kg of manure a day, plus litres of urine. In New York City, estimates from the 1890s suggest horses left about 2.5 million pounds (more than 1,100 tonnes) of manure and about 60,000 gallons of urine on the streets every single day.

In dry weather the manure was ground into dust by wheels and blown into people's eyes, homes and food. In wet weather it became a slippery, stinking slush. Huge piles collected in vacant lots and outside stables, and they bred enormous numbers of flies, which carried germs to kitchens and markets. Doctors at the time worried that this filth helped spread diseases. When horses were worked to exhaustion or fell ill, they sometimes died right in the street, and their bodies could lie there until someone came to haul them away to be turned into glue and fertiliser.

Horses also caused traffic jams and accidents. A frightened horse could bolt, dragging a heavy wagon through a crowd, and many people were hurt by kicks, falls and runaway carts. Feeding and stabling all those animals was expensive too: horses needed hay and oats every day, whether they worked or not, and city stables took up a lot of valuable land.

New York tried hard to clean up. In 1895 the city's new street-cleaning chief, George E. Waring Jr., set up a corps of workers in white uniforms who swept the streets every day with brooms and carts. He also got a law passed saying that horses and carts had to be kept in stables overnight rather than left in the street. Manure was sold as fertiliser and dead horses went to glue factories. The streets became dramatically cleaner, and the city even held a parade in 1896 to celebrate the sweepers.

You may have heard a famous story that in 1894 a London newspaper predicted the city would be buried under nine feet of manure by 1950. It is a great story, but historians have searched for that newspaper article and never found it, so it is best treated as a modern myth. The real problem was serious enough without exaggeration.

So when the first cars appeared, many people saw them as the clean, modern answer. A car did not leave manure, did not attract flies, did not need feeding when it was parked and could not bolt in fright. An Italian newspaper in 1896 even looked forward to cars removing manure from the streets. Nobody yet worried about what came out of the exhaust pipe; that story comes in Part 17. The change happened fast. In 1890 the United States had about 13,800 companies building horse-drawn carriages. By 1920 only about 90 were left. By 1929 there were about 23 million cars registered in the United States, and the horse had almost disappeared from city streets.

sections.heading: Moving to the Suburbs
paragraphs: Before cars, most city workers had to live close to their jobs. If you walked to work, you could live perhaps half an hour's walk away. In the late 1800s, horse-drawn streetcars and then electric streetcars let people move a bit farther out. Developers built neighbourhoods along the streetcar lines, called streetcar suburbs, with narrow plots, houses with front porches, and shops clustered near the stops. An electric streetcar could cover in about ten minutes a distance that took half an hour to walk. Driveways and garages were rare, because hardly anyone had a car.

The car changed the shape of cities. A family with a car no longer needed to live near a streetcar line or a railway station. They could live almost anywhere a road went. From the 1920s, and especially after World War II, new suburbs were designed around the car: wide curving streets, houses with garages and driveways, and homes spread out on bigger plots of land, often far from shops and offices.

After the war, millions of soldiers came home, married and started families, and they needed houses. The US government helped them borrow money cheaply through the GI Bill and government-backed mortgages. Builders bought farmland outside cities and put up whole new towns of nearly identical houses. The most famous was Levittown, on Long Island near New York. Between 1947 and 1951 the company Levitt and Sons built more than 17,000 homes there, using assembly-line methods borrowed from car factories: teams of workers moved from house to house, each doing one job. By July 1948 they were finishing about 30 houses a day.

Levittown also shows the unfair side of this story. Its early house rules said homes could be lived in only by white people, and Black families, including war veterans, were turned away. Many other suburbs and banks of the time also kept Black Americans out, through rules and practices that historians call housing discrimination. So the dream of a suburban home with a car in the driveway was not open to everyone.

Suburbs grew enormously. In the decade after the war the United States built more than a million new homes a year, several times the rate of the Depression years before. People who lived in the suburbs drove to work, drove to the shops, and drove their children to school and to friends' houses. A second car started to seem normal.

Shopping changed too. Instead of walking to a busy downtown street, suburban families drove to shopping centres surrounded by vast car parks. On 8 October 1956 Southdale Center opened in Edina, Minnesota, near Minneapolis. Designed by the architect Victor Gruen, it was the first fully enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall in the United States, warm in the freezing Minnesota winter and cool in summer. Its plans included about 5,200 parking spaces. Hundreds of new shopping centres opened across the United States every year in the late 1950s. Downtown shops in many cities began to struggle as customers drove out to the malls.

sections.heading: Motels, Drive-Ins and the Great Road Trip
paragraphs: Cars did not only change where people lived. They created brand-new kinds of places that simply could not have existed before.

Take the motel. In the early days of motoring, a family driving a long way might camp by the road or stay in a grand hotel in the middle of a city, where you had to find somewhere to park and carry your bags through a fancy lobby. In California, an architect named Arthur Heineman had a better idea. He noticed that driving from Los Angeles to San Francisco took about two days, so travellers needed a place to stop halfway. In San Luis Obispo, roughly at the midpoint, he built a roadside inn where guests could park right outside their own room. It opened on 12 December 1925 as the Milestone Mo-Tel. The name joined 'motor' and 'hotel' together, and the word 'motel' was born.

The Milestone Mo-Tel looked like a Spanish mission, with white walls, red-tiled roofs and a bell tower. Every unit had its own bathroom with a shower, and a room cost 1.25 dollars a night. Thousands of motels followed along highways like Route 66, with bright neon signs, swimming pools and names promising comfort to tired drivers. Parts of the original building, including its bell tower, still stand.

Eating changed too. In 1921 Kirby's Pig Stand opened in Dallas, Texas, and is considered the first drive-in restaurant. Instead of going inside, customers parked, and waiters called carhops came out to take orders and bring food to the car, sometimes on trays that hooked onto the car window. Drive-in restaurants were especially popular in the 1950s and 1960s. Later, drive-through windows let people order and collect food without even parking, an idea that helped fast-food chains spread across the world.

Then there were movies under the stars. Richard Hollingshead, from a family that ran a chemical company in Camden, New Jersey, tested an idea in the driveway of his home in Riverton, New Jersey, in 1932: he put a film projector on the hood of his car and nailed a screen to trees in his garden. He received a patent for his drive-in theatre in May 1933, and on 6 June 1933 he opened the first one in Pennsauken, near Camden. It had space for about 400 cars and a screen about 12 by 15 metres. Families could watch from their own car seats, and his advertising promised that the whole family was welcome, however noisy the children were. The first film shown was a comedy called Wives Beware.

Hollingshead's own theatre did not make money, and he sold it after three years. But the idea took off. Drive-in theatres peaked in the late 1950s, when there were more than 4,000 of them in the United States.

Put all of these together, and you get one of the great inventions of the car age: the family road trip. Parents piled children, suitcases and picnic baskets into the car and set off to see national parks, beaches and famous sights, eating at roadside diners and sleeping in motels along the way. Travel that once needed train tickets and timetables could now begin whenever a family wanted, from their own front door.

sections.heading: No More Lonely Farms
paragraphs: In 1900 most Americans, and most people around the world, lived in the countryside. For a farm family, the nearest town might be 10 or 20 kilometres away along a dirt road. With a horse and wagon, a trip to town to buy supplies, sell eggs or visit the doctor could take most of a day, so families went only when they had to. Children often could not attend school beyond the small one-room schoolhouse within walking distance. In winter, when roads were deep in snow or mud, some families hardly saw anyone else for weeks.

Mail was the first link to the wider world. In the United States, the Post Office began Rural Free Delivery in 1896, starting with routes in Jefferson County, West Virginia. Instead of travelling to a distant post office, farm families could have letters, newspapers and catalogues brought to a mailbox at the end of their lane. In 1913 the Post Office added parcel post, so families could order clothes, tools and even seeds from mail-order companies like Sears, Roebuck and Company and have them delivered. By 1930, more than 43,000 rural routes served nearly 6.9 million families. Mail carriers were some of the first country people to switch from horses to motor vehicles, and the government's interest in good routes for the mail helped persuade Congress to pay for better rural roads, starting with a federal road law in 1916.

The car, especially the cheap and tough Model T, made the biggest difference. Suddenly a 20 km trip to town took less than an hour. Farmers could drive their produce to market and bring back supplies the same morning. Families could go to church, visit relatives, attend county fairs and go to the cinema. Young people from different farms could meet much more easily, and many found friends, and husbands and wives, from farther away than their parents ever could.

Farmers also found clever ways to use their cars as machines. With the rear wheels jacked up, a belt could be run from a wheel to a saw, a water pump or a butter churn, so the car's engine did farm work. Some companies sold kits to turn a Model T into a small tractor.

Health care changed too. A country doctor with a car could make house calls to many more patients in a day and could reach an emergency much faster. Sick or injured people could be driven to a hospital in town. Over the following decades, motor buses also made it possible to close many tiny one-room schools and carry children to larger schools with more teachers, more subjects and better equipment, although some communities were sad to lose their small local school.

sections.heading: Freedom Behind the Wheel
paragraphs: For many people, the car meant independence. Nobody showed that more clearly than women. You have already met Bertha Benz, who made the first long-distance car journey in 1888 at a time when, as a married woman, she was not allowed to hold her husband's patent and women could not study at university in her part of Germany. In 1909, as Part 10 told, Alice Ramsey became the first woman to drive across the United States.

By the 1920s, especially after the electric self-starter (Part 7) ended the need for heavy hand-cranking, millions of women were driving. Carmakers began advertising directly to them. A woman with a car could take a job farther from home, run a business, visit friends and family when she chose, or simply go for a drive on her own. In a time when many women were still expected to stay at home, that was a big change, and it came in the same years that women in the United States and Britain won the right to vote.

But freedom on the road was not shared equally. In the United States, from the late 1800s until the 1960s, many states and towns enforced segregation, laws and customs that separated Black and white Americans and treated Black people unfairly. For Black families, a road trip could be stressful and even dangerous. Many hotels, restaurants and gas stations refused to serve Black customers. Some places were known as 'sundown towns', where Black people were warned to leave before dark. Running out of fuel or needing a room for the night in the wrong place could put a family at risk.

Victor Hugo Green (1892–1960), a Black postal worker living in Harlem in New York City, decided to help. In 1936 he published a small guidebook listing businesses that welcomed Black travellers: hotels, guest houses, restaurants, petrol stations, barber shops and more. The first edition covered only the New York area. It was so useful that it grew year after year, eventually covering much of the United States and parts of Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean and Bermuda. It was called The Negro Motorist Green Book, and later simply The Green Book.

The guide was sold by mail and through churches and Black-owned businesses, and also at Esso gas stations, one of the few big companies that supported it. At its peak about 15,000 copies were printed each year. Many families kept one in the glove compartment for every trip. In its introduction, Green wrote that he hoped 'there will be a day sometime in the near future when this guide will not have to be published.'

That day came closer when the Civil Rights Act of 1964 made it illegal for businesses like hotels and restaurants to refuse customers because of their race. After Green died in 1960, Alma Green and the staff kept the guide going, and the last edition appeared in 1966–67. Published from 1936 to 1966, the Green Book is now remembered as both a clever, practical tool and a powerful reminder that the open road was not open to everyone.

sections.heading: Streets for Cars, Not People
paragraphs: As the number of cars grew, cities changed to make room for them, and not always for the better. Before cars, a city street was a shared space. Children played in it, sellers set up stalls, people stopped to chat, and walkers crossed wherever they liked. As fast cars filled the roads, the street became a dangerous place to be. In the 1920s, as cars knocked down many pedestrians, especially children, cities and car groups began telling walkers to stay on the pavement and cross only at marked crossings. People who crossed carelessly were mocked as 'jaywalkers'. Little by little, the road became a place for cars, and people were pushed to its edges.

Public transport suffered too. America's streetcar systems were huge in the early 1900s, with tens of thousands of miles of track, and streetcar ridership peaked around the early 1920s. After that, as more people bought cars, ridership fell almost every year. Many companies were already in financial trouble because fares were fixed by law while costs rose. During the 1930s and 1940s, most US cities replaced their streetcars with buses or let them close.

You may hear that General Motors secretly destroyed America's streetcars. The real story is more complicated. In 1949 General Motors, Firestone, Standard Oil of California and other companies were convicted of conspiring to monopolise the sale of buses and supplies to transit companies they had invested in, and GM was fined just 5,000 dollars. But most transport historians think streetcars were already declining for many reasons, especially the popularity of the car, rising costs and fixed fares, the Great Depression, and government road building, and that GM took advantage of a decline that was already happening.

The biggest scars came from highways. When the new Interstates of Part 13 reached cities in the 1950s and 1960s, planners often ran them straight through existing neighbourhoods, knocking down homes, shops and churches. Very often the neighbourhoods chosen were poorer ones, and many were Black communities, where people had less political power to fight back. Some neighbourhoods were split in two by huge concrete roads, cutting people off from their neighbours, schools and shops.

Not everyone accepted this. In the 1960s and 1970s, protests sometimes called 'freeway revolts' stopped or changed planned highways in cities such as San Francisco, Boston and New York. In New York, the writer and activist Jane Jacobs helped lead campaigns against a planned expressway across Lower Manhattan, which was eventually abandoned. Today some cities are even removing old elevated highways and replacing them with streets, parks and homes.

Parking took up space too. Every car needs somewhere to sit when it is not moving, which is most of the time, so cities built car parks, garages and wide streets lined with parked cars. Downtown buildings were sometimes torn down to make surface parking lots. Planners still argue about how to balance the needs of drivers with those of people walking, cycling and riding buses and trains.

sections.heading: Cars Go to War
paragraphs: Cars and trucks changed warfare too. One of the most famous stories comes from the start of World War I. In early September 1914 the German army was advancing towards Paris. The French commander of the city's defences, General Joseph Gallieni, needed to rush extra soldiers to the front line. On the night of 7 to 8 September, about 600 Paris taxicabs, many of them small Renault cabs, were gathered at Les Invalides and sent to carry soldiers about 50 km towards the fighting near Nanteuil-le-Haudouin, during the First Battle of the Marne. The drivers kept their meters running, and the French government later paid the fares, about 70,000 francs in total.

These 'Taxis of the Marne' became a legend in France, a symbol of ordinary people helping to save their country. Historians today point out that the taxis carried only a small part of the troops and probably did not change the outcome of the battle, which was decided by much larger movements of soldiers by train and on foot. But the boost to French spirits was real, and the story showed something new: motor vehicles could move people faster than an army had ever moved them before.

In World War II, the most famous military car was the Jeep. In 1940 the US Army asked carmakers for a small, tough, four-wheel-drive scout car and gave them just 49 days to build a prototype. A small company called American Bantam, with designer Karl Probst, built the first one, and Willys-Overland and Ford developed their own. Willys's version, the MB, became the standard design, and Ford also built it as the GPW. Together they made about 640,000 Jeeps. They carried officers, pulled small guns, and served as ambulances. Nobody is quite sure where the name 'Jeep' came from; one popular idea is that it came from 'GP', short for 'general purpose', but that has never been proven. After the war, the Jeep became a civilian off-road vehicle, an ancestor of today's SUVs.

sections.heading: A World on Wheels
paragraphs: Step back and look at how much changed in a single lifetime. A child born in 1890 grew up in a city full of horses, with muddy streets and long walks to everywhere. By the time that child was 40, in 1930, there were about 23 million cars in the United States alone. By the time they were 70, in 1960, families lived in suburbs, shopped in malls, ate at drive-ins, slept in motels and crossed the country on highways.

The same transformation spread around the world, sometimes faster, sometimes slower. In Europe, cheap small cars after World War II, like those in Part 12, put millions of families on the road. Today there are roughly one and a half billion motor vehicles in the world, although estimates vary. Many people's daily lives, from how they get to school to where their food comes from, depend on cars and trucks.

But the car brought more than convenience. It also brought a new thrill: speed. From the very beginning, some people did not want to just get somewhere. They wanted to get there first, faster than anyone had ever gone before. And they were willing to risk everything to do it. In the next part, we head to the racetrack.

deepDive: Historians often describe what cars did to cities with the idea of a 'travel time budget'. Studies in many countries suggest people tend to spend roughly an hour a day travelling, whatever technology they use. When people walked, that hour kept cities compact, a few kilometres across. Streetcars stretched cities along their lines, and cars let them spread in every direction, which is one reason suburbs grew so fast. Car-based growth also relied on public policy, not just personal choice. In the United States, government-backed mortgages, the tax-funded Interstates and zoning rules that separated homes from shops all favoured spread-out, car-dependent suburbs. Historians have documented how mortgage maps and lending rules in the 1930s and later marked many Black neighbourhoods as risky, a practice called redlining, while suburbs like Levittown used racial covenants to exclude Black buyers; the Supreme Court ruled in 1948 (Shelley v. Kraemer) that courts could not enforce such covenants, but discrimination continued in other ways. The 'horse problem' is often used as a lesson about technology, but carefully. The urban horse really was a public-health headache, yet the famous 1894 prediction of nine feet of manure is not supported by any known newspaper. The real lesson may be that the car solved one pollution problem while creating others, such as exhaust, noise, traffic deaths and land given over to parking. Debates about the streetcar 'conspiracy' show how history can be argued. Writer Bradford Snell's 1974 testimony to the US Senate claimed a deliberate plot, but economists and transport historians such as George Hilton argued that streetcars were losing money long before GM got involved. Most scholars now see GM's actions as real but limited, affecting perhaps a tenth of US transit systems. Finally, cars changed social life in ways that are hard to measure: courtship, the teenage driving licence as a coming-of-age moment, and new kinds of freedom that were, for decades, not shared fairly.
funFact: The world's first motel, the Milestone Mo-Tel in San Luis Obispo, California, opened in 1925 and charged 1.25 dollars a night.

check.q: What was the Negro Motorist Green Book?
check.a: A guidebook (1936–1966) listing places that welcomed Black travellers during segregation
wrong: A road atlas showing all the new Interstate highways
A rulebook for the first driving tests
A catalogue for ordering cars by mail
